name: Cordycepin

lead: Cordycepin is a compound made by the Cordyceps militaris fungus. People take Cordyceps supplements hoping for better energy and recovery, which in turn could help them train more and look more athletic.

Most research on cordycepin itself is in cells and animals, covering inflammation, cancer cells and the brain. Human trials have tested C. militaris preparations, such as immune-response studies in healthy adults.

paras: Cordycepin reaches consumers as Cordyceps militaris powders, extracts and beverages rather than as an isolated product. The fungus is used in traditional Chinese medicine and cooked in Asian dishes.

Wikipedia notes that C. militaris supplements lack sufficient scientific evidence for safety or effectiveness and that product quality varies. Cordycepin has a short half-life, reported as 1 to 2 hours in cell culture.

angle.text: Users describe Cordyceps products as an energy and recovery support. The appearance link runs through training volume; no published trial cited here tests physique outcomes.

lead: Cordycepin (3'-deoxyadenosine) is a derivative of adenosine first reported in 1950 from cultures of Cordyceps militaris. [1] It is the signature compound of the fungus marketed in supplements, which people take for energy and recovery that may support training. [2]

Research on cordycepin is mostly laboratory and animal work, including inflammation, kinase signalling in cancer cells and neuroprotection. [3][4] Human trials have studied C. militaris preparations on immune function in healthy adults. [5][6]

paras: Cordycepin differs from adenosine by a hydrogen in place of the 3' hydroxyl group. It is produced by C. militaris and a few related fungi and is also made synthetically. A four-gene cluster characterised in 2017 produces it alongside pentostatin, which protects it from breakdown. [1]

Because it resembles adenosine, some enzymes treat it as adenosine, which can disrupt RNA synthesis. Studies report links to circadian clock resetting in mice and to anti-inflammatory effects. It crosses the blood-brain barrier and has a short half-life. [1] Reviews describe kinase pathways targeted in cancer cells, including AMPK, mTOR and MAPK. [3]

Cordyceps militaris is used in traditional Chinese medicine and eaten in soups and hot pot in Asia; China has approved it as a novel food. [7] It is sold as a supplement, and Wikipedia states its health claims lack sufficient scientific evidence. [7]

A randomized controlled trial of a C. militaris beverage examined immune responses in healthy adults. [5] A Korean randomized trial of C. militaris in healthy men examined cell-mediated immunity and safety. [6] Phase 1 trials registered the combination of cordycepin with pentostatin in leukemia, and a trial of a cordycepin-derived drug, NUC-7738, in advanced cancers is recruiting. [8][9] A registered trial of ginseng and Cordyceps will examine aerobic capacity in healthy people. [10]
